title: Andy Burnham 'really concerned' if Man City owners sell up after rule breaches
description: Andy Burnham has said he would be "really concerned" if Manchester City's owners decide to sell up after the club was found guilty of Premier League f
body: Andy Burnham has said he would be "really concerned" if Manchester City's owners decide to sell up after the club was found guilty of Premier League financial rule breaches.The prime minister said the situation was "contested by Manchester City" and he praised the club's owners since 2008 - led by Sheikh Mansour, United Arab Emirates deputy prime minister and royal family member - for investing in Manchester.An independent commission found the club guilty of the majority of the 115 charges they faced, a verdict that City are expected to appeal.The club continue to deny any wrongdoing and have until 2 October to submit an appeal.It comes as the Independent Football Regulator – set up by the government in 2025 – said the case had raised "serious issues".The regulator suggested it would be exploring options – including whether to strip the owners of their licence to own the club – once the disciplinary process was completed.Among the independent panel's findings were that City arranged "sham contracts" with a number of commercial partners as part of a scheme to disguise secret funding of more than £830m.The Premier League said City "systematically broke Premier League Rules for nearly a decade".The independent panel will hold a sanctions hearing – which could take months to convene – to decide the punishment. City can appeal both the guilty verdicts and the sanction, leaving City and the league in a state of chaos and uncertainty.The punishment could range from a huge fine, being deducted points or ejected from the Premier League, to being stripped of the eight trophies they had won in the affected period.Some fans and pundits have questioned how the club's owners can carry on if they deliberately breached rules over the course of nine years.Asked by the BBC's political editor Chris Mason if he was concerned that Manchester City's owners would now sell the club, Burham said on Wednesday: "I would be really concerned to lose them."They've been such a huge partner in the building of modern Manchester and obviously the building of Manchester City into the global force that it is."Burnham, the mayor of Greater Manchester until June, added: "I do actually thank the City Football Group and the wider ownership for the money that they didn't just put into the Etihad [Stadium] and the campus around it but also into the city".He said he was "of course" confident that his own interactions with City's owners when he was mayor would stand up to scrutiny.Burnham made his comments amid widespread shock in football about the scale of the independent commission's findings – and the strength of Premier League comments about City's actions.Burnham was speaking to the BBC from Hill Dickinson Stadium, the home of Everton, the team he supports.Everton had their own run in with Premier League financial rules when they were charged and deducted 10 points for more minor breaches in November 2023, reduced to six on appeal.Burnham said: "Everton was in this position a few years ago and you might remember that I fought for Everton in that situation because I still hold the view very firmly that they weren't fairly treated in that process."Drawing a comparison between that and City's current predicament, he added: "I remember people proclaiming Everton guilty at the time and with hindsight I think more people would say that wasn't fair, the way that was handled."So it would be wrong of me to leap to one side given the experience that I'd had before becoming prime minister."It is "frustrating when people rush to judgement", Burnham said.He accepted there was "a lot at stake" for City fans, the club and Manchester itself.But he added it would be wrong for him to intervene.City have said in a statement they are "both disappointed and surprised by the opinion of the Premier League Commission" and maintained their innocence of all the accusations made.

schema.headline: Andy Burnham 'really concerned' if Man City owners sell up after rule breaches

title: Conservatives pledge 'tough love' benefit rules for under-25s
description: The Conservatives have said they would introduce new work requirements for under-25s claiming benefits in a "tough love" approach to youth joblessness
body: The Conservatives have said they would introduce new work requirements for under-25s claiming benefits in a "tough love" approach to youth joblessness.Young people claiming Universal Credit who are fit to work but have not worked for six months continuously would face new rules to qualify for payments, including daily attendance at a job centre or courses.The party says the scheme would help tackle the almost one million people aged 16 to 24 in the UK who are not in education, employment or training, known as Neets.But anti-poverty charity Trussell warned that people on Universal Credit could not afford basic essentials, which harmed their ability to find and keep work.Under the Tory proposals, those aged 18 to 24 who apply for Universal Credit but have not previously worked for a continuous period of six months or more, for at least 16 hours per week, would instead have to take part in a "Get to Work" scheme.Rather than Universal Credit, they would receive a "Get to Work Allowance" paid at the same rate but requiring daily attendance at a job centre, on work experience or work readiness courses.They would be assigned a manager and have to take part in job search workshops and interview preparation sessions.The programme would last six months, or less if a participant secures a job - but those who are still unemployed after half a year on the scheme would have their benefit cut by 30%.Young people on Universal Credit who have previously worked for six months, have health issues or care responsibilities or are estranged would be exempt.The party has also said it would look closer at whether parents' earnings and savings should be factored into welfare payments for their children.Shadow work and pensions secretary Helen Whately said the measures were designed to "show some tough love" to reduce the number of Neets."Too many young people are leaving school and signing straight onto benefits - this is a waste of their potential and a disaster for our economy," the Tory MP said.

schema.headline: Conservatives pledge 'tough love' benefit rules for under-25s

title: Flydubai passenger describes putting attacker in chokehold after cockpit stabbing
description: Passengers on a flight to Israel have recounted how they subdued a pilot after he stabbed the other pilot and appeared to be trying to disable the pla
body: Passengers on a flight to Israel have recounted how they subdued a pilot after he stabbed the other pilot and appeared to be trying to disable the plane, while others described the "terrifying" moment they thought they would die.Appearing in a bloodstained shirt after the ordeal, Yaniv Hayun told Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu he realised something was wrong when the aircraft suddenly dropped. The plane, en route from Dubai to Tel Aviv, plummeted 17,000ft (5,200m) in less than two minutes."Someone screamed... the light went out," Hayun said in a video posted by the prime minister on social media.He and others tried to push open the cockpit door, but the pilot who had been stabbed was very close to it, so it was hard to open. Before he collapsed, the injured pilot managed to open the door.When Hayun and another man entered the cockpit, he said he saw one pilot down and the attacker on the instruments, between the two seats, "trying to destroy the instruments in order to...disable the plane"."I grabbed the attacker, put him in a chokehold, and pulled him - first and foremost - outside," Hayun said."We pulled him out; it was a matter of seconds. I called out to the Israeli guys with us on the plane - I called them, and two other guys came over to me... we pinned [the attacker] down to keep him secure."The Flydubai flight eventually landed at Tabuk airport in northwestern Saudi Arabia, and the passengers were later taken to Tel Aviv's Ben Gurion airport on a repatriation aircraft.They were greeted by crowds of onlookers playing music, singing, dancing and waving Israeli flags."Thank God I'm alive," passenger Haim Lazarovich told journalists, adding that "the most terrifying moment in this flight was when the pilot loses control".Oran Choen, an 18-year-old passenger, described the incident as "a very tough moment"."Maybe it was five minutes, but it feels like hell - I heard my brother behind me scream that we was going to die," he added.A paramedic from Israel's ambulance service later told the BBC that a number of people were "very emotional and crying as they came off the plane". The stabbed pilot, Indian national Captain Smit Machchhar, was taken to hospital but is in stable condition, according to the Indian embassy in Saudi Arabia. Netanyahu praised Machchhar as a "true hero" of "extraordinary bravery".The attacker was arrested and is being questioned by Saudi authorities. Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz has called it an "attempted jihadist terror attack". No official motive for the incident or further information has been given.US President Donald Trump said he had spoken with Netanyahu following the incident, saying it seemed as though the attacker was "perhaps a terrorist" or there were other reasons behind the attack.

schema.headline: Flydubai passenger describes putting attacker in chokehold after cockpit stabbing

title: Dame Esther Rantzen dies aged 86
description: Dame Esther Rantzen, who presented BBC show That's Life! for 21 years and launched the charity Childline, has died at the age of 86.Prime Minister And
body: Dame Esther Rantzen, who presented BBC show That's Life! for 21 years and launched the charity Childline, has died at the age of 86.Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the veteran broadcaster and campaigner had "changed countless lives".Dame Esther hosted and produced That's Life! during its run from 1973 to 1994. It regularly attracted 20 million viewers for its mixture of serious consumer investigations and light-hearted items.She launched Childline, a British counselling service for children and young people, in 1986, and in 2013 she launched Silver Line to help elderly people suffering from isolation and loneliness. Later in life, she became a prominent campaigner for the legalisation of assisted dying.She had been terminally ill with lung cancer. In December 2023, she revealed she had joined Dignitas, the Swiss assisted dying clinic.But in a statement given to the Press Association earlier this month, she said that despite having "spent the money and made the plans" to go to Dignitas, she had since reached the point where she was "too physically fragile to make the journey".She added that the law must "change and change quickly", as she renewed her plea ahead of the latest debate and vote on the Terminally Ill Adults (End of Life) Bill, which failed to pass through the Commons.Rantzen joined BBC radio as a sound effects assistant before becoming a TV researcher, and in 1968 she trained as a producer and director.The young broadcaster became a researcher and reporter for Bernard Braden's consumer affairs programme, Braden's Week.When That's Life! launched in 1973, she was its figurehead and became a popular fixture on screens as the show's formidable and fun-loving presenter and producer.The consumer show's notable items, according to her website, external, included "talking dogs, Jobsworth Awards and campaigns on behalf of abused children, organ transplants, safe playgrounds, and to provide justice for consumers".Its most-viewed episode featured Sir Nicholas Winton being introduced for the first time to survivors he had saved from the Holocaust, during a 1988 instalment of the show.Later in her career, she also appeared on Strictly Come Dancing, First Dates and I'm a Celebrity... Get Me Out of Here!Dame Esther was married to documentary film-maker Desmond Wilcox from 1977 until he died in 2000. They had three children.She was made a dame in 2015 for her services to children and older people.Figures from politics, broadcasting and the charity sector have paid tribute to Dame Esther for her impact on public life.The prime minister said he would "always admire the characteristic courage and openness with which she spoke about her illness, making us all think about the difficult questions we face at the end of life".BBC director-general Matt Brittin paid tribute to Dame Esther as a "legend of British broadcasting" whose contribution to public life was "immeasurable"."Her warmth, spirit and fight for justice and action that we saw on our screens continued long after the programme ended, with a lifetime of campaigning where she changed the lives of millions," he said.Kim Leadbeater, the Labour MP who sponsored the assisted dying bill, told the BBC that Dame Esther was a "wonderful mix of strength and feistiness, but also really deep compassion and kindness" - and that she would continue to inspire campaigners.Chris Sherwood, the chief executive of the NSPCC, which runs the Childline helpline, said Dame Esther had gone to "exceptional lengths to ensure children and young people across the UK had somewhere to turn when they were in need of help".Dame Esther's That's Life! co-presenter Bill Buckley told the BBC's Radio 4 Front Row programme that "nothing would stop her" when it came to campaigning."She saw the light at the end of the tunnel and followed it doggedly," he said.Watch Katie Razzall's half-hour special programme Esther! on iPlayer. It will also be shown this Friday, 2 October, on BBC One at 19:30 BST.

title: Lola Young: Vaping making it harder to breathe, singer says
description: Hills, who helps artists with their vocals, says vaping can have an impact on an artist's voice and struggling to breathe can risk straining your voic
body: Hills, who helps artists with their vocals, says vaping can have an impact on an artist's voice and struggling to breathe can risk straining your voice. "Vaping may not affect the voice box just itself, it affects the lungs, the airways, the throat - it's all respiratory, it's all connected. So doing that can affect your vocal technique," she says."Breathing is really important. Singing requires controlled inhalation and sustained, efficient exhalation. "You end up trying harder, putting in more effort for the same results you were getting beforehand."She adds that when artists struggle with their voice, it can have significant psychological impacts on them too. "They can feel like they've lost themselves," she says. "It can become quite a big deal emotionally."Overall, she wouldn't recommend vaping to her clients."As a performer, as an artist, you want to stay in the best health you can for your voice to work at its best."We all know it's not the healthy choice and if you can avoid it - absolutely."Young returned to the spotlight earlier this year following a five-month hiatus after she collapsed on stage.She has been open in the past about her struggles with her health and addiction, previously telling The Guardian, external about dealing with cocaine dependency.She has also struggled with her mental health and was diagnosed with schizoaffective disorder and ADHD when she was a teenager. BBC Newsbeat has contacted Young's representatives for comment.

schema.headline: Lola Young: Vaping making it harder to breathe, singer says

title: Cristiano Ronaldo leaves Portugal camp after boss Jorge Jesus denies rift
description: Cristiano Ronaldo says he has left Portugal's international camp and will explain the reasons why "in time".It comes after head coach Jorge Jesus earl
body: Cristiano Ronaldo says he has left Portugal's international camp and will explain the reasons why "in time".It comes after head coach Jorge Jesus earlier said there was no rift with the captain, following claims the five-times Ballon d'Or winner had refused to train.Ronaldo has said he considered retiring from international football after the World Cup in the summer but opted to continue as he chases down 1,000 career goals.He was included in Jesus' 25-man squad for the current international break and started the opening Nations League game against Wales.However, the Al-Nassr forward did not feature in Portugal's 2-1 win over Norway in Olso on Sunday and did not join his team-mates in going over to the visiting fans at the final whistle.Instead, the former Real Madrid and Manchester United player headed to the changing rooms - prompting reports he was unhappy with the manager.Speaking to media before Portugal's Nations League match against Denmark on Thursday, Jesus said: "There was no incident whatsoever."Any player - and I was a player myself - when you spend 20 or 30 minutes warming up and then don't get on, no-one is happy about that."Jesus said he had told Ronaldo before the match he would not be starting, but might be brought on later in the game."Afterwards, as coach, I decided not to bring him on. It's nothing to make a fuss about," he added.Former Benfica manager Jesus also dismissed suggestions Ronaldo had refused to train on Tuesday, saying the 41-year-old instead had to do individual exercises for "mobility" and "strengthening" but would train as normal on Wednesday.However, Ronaldo did not join his team-mates on the pitch in Denmark with Portuguese media sharing a video of him leaving Parken stadium alongside two members of the backroom staff.And the player later took to Instagram to announce his departure."After the press conference of the national team and following a conversation with the president of the Portuguese Football Federation, I have decided to leave the national team training camp," he wrote."In time, I will tell all the Portuguese the truth about the reasons that motivated me to leave."He added he wished his team-mates good luck in their forthcoming games.Goncalo Ramos scored the winner against Norway and Jesus had said the AC Milan striker would again be preferred to Ronaldo against Denmark."If I need [Ronaldo], he'll come on. If I don't need him, he won't."The Portuguese Football Federation later confirmed Ronaldo's departure in a statement which added: "Preparation for the two matches against Denmark and Norway continue as planned with the 24 remaining squad members."The entire delegation remains totally focussed on the national team's next fixtures and on achieving the established objectives."

schema.headline: Cristiano Ronaldo leaves Portugal camp after boss Jorge Jesus denies rift

title: Tapestry tour will include audio-described guide for blind people
description: Osman, who has no sight in either eye, contacted the museum via solicitor Leigh Day to ask whether audio-described tours would be available.The law fi
body: Osman, who has no sight in either eye, contacted the museum via solicitor Leigh Day to ask whether audio-described tours would be available.The law firm told him the museum had said self-guided visits would be prioritised over tours and events.The British Museum said this was because there are limits on how many hours of light to which the tapestry can be exposed - and this in turn restricted visitor numbers.Osman is seeking damages and a declaration that he was discriminated against and an order requiring the museum to change its policies.He also said relevant staff should be given disability awareness training and he hoped the legal action would "help make sure blind and partially sighted people are properly considered" when major exhibitions are planned.His solicitor said the Equality Act placed obligations on service providers to anticipate the needs of disabled people and take reasonable steps to avoid substantial disadvantage."Our client is asking for the same opportunity as sighted visitors to experience this exhibition."A British Museum spokesperson said the museum was "committed to making the Bayeux Tapestry exhibition as accessible as possible" and had worked with specialist access consultants.Provisions currently include a sensory map to help visitors prepare for their visit, as well as dedicated tours during the exhibition run which will include an in-person audio-described tour, the spokesperson said."We are also exploring including a separate audio-described tour as part of the exhibition's app-based audio guide."The 70m (230ft) embroidery, which depicts the events leading up to the Norman Conquest of 1066, is on loan from France and is on display at the museum until 11 July 2027.Listen to the best of BBC Radio London on Sounds and follow BBC London on Facebook, external, X, external and Instagram, external. Send your story ideas to hello.bbclondon@bbc.co.uk, external

schema.headline: Tapestry tour will include audio-described guide for blind people

title: Brendan Venter: Saracens' 'wine consultant' misses another press conference
description: Saracens head coach Joe Shaw has refused to say when, or if, director of rugby Brendan Venter will speak to the media again, despite the club facing f
body: Saracens head coach Joe Shaw has refused to say when, or if, director of rugby Brendan Venter will speak to the media again, despite the club facing fines for him not doing so.Venter was not at Wednesday's pre-match press conference for their forthcoming game with Sale after not attending Prem Rugby's pre-season launch day, or doing any media duties before, during or after the opening-weekend victory at Leicester.The Daily Telegraph reported on Tuesday that Venter had "resigned" as director of rugby and taken up a new role as "head of rugby culture and wine consultant", but this has not been confirmed by the club nor Prem Rugby.When asked if Venter would resume media duties, as part of his responsibilities as a director of rugby, Shaw said: "I'm just going to talk about the rugby. "I'll leave the club to talk about where we stand on all those kind of things."BBC Sport has contacted Saracens for comment.It is understood Sarries have already been fined £5,000 after Venter was not present at the Prem's pre-season launch day.It is also thought a change of job title would not preclude Venter from his contractual responsibilities.Saracens announced in January that Venter would be returning as director of rugby and have yet to publicly confirm any change to his day-to-day responsibilities.He succeeded Mark McCall, who stepped down at the end of last season after 15 years in the job.

schema.headline: Brendan Venter: Saracens' 'wine consultant' misses another press conference

title: Social anxiety: The hidden habits that make it worse - and how you can break them
description: Mary, who is now 25, describes her social anxiety as like an out of body experience. When she was talking to new people, heat would rise in her face a
body: Mary, who is now 25, describes her social anxiety as like an out of body experience. When she was talking to new people, heat would rise in her face and her hands would begin to tingle. "I'd almost feel myself separating from my body. I forgot how to form words," she says."After social situations I was often left with the sense that I'd done something awful. I had an all-consuming feel of shame. I kept thinking there was something fundamentally flawed in me."Neil Greening, chair of the Social Anxiety Alliance UK, says this is a typical characteristic of people with social anxiety."People think they have a personality flaw. They internalise it rather than seeing it as a recognisable condition that they can get help for."The key thing to remember: It's fairly normal to feel a little shy or anxious when meeting new people, being in new situations or going for a job interview. Social anxiety is when it actually stops people doing things, Greening says.For those with a clinical diagnosis it can have a debilitating impact like it did for Mary."It can be hard to admit to any form of social anxiety in a world where extrovertism and social confidence is generally admired. Many people try to hide their social anxiety or use safety behaviours."Signs someone may be socially anxious:Keeping quietGiving short answersPlaying with a phone to avoid interactingAlways staying close to someone or staying on the edges of a groupSticking to safe subjects of conversation like workGreening says there is some evidence social anxiety is getting worse and that increased use of smartphones and remote working is contributing by "leading to less social interactions and increased levels of anxiety".Mary, who has moved on to do a postgraduate course, is now managing her social anxiety better. After her undergraduate degree she got support from the NHS in the form of a talking therapy called CBT.It is considered the gold standard treatment for social anxiety and encourages people to re-frame their thoughts and change their behaviours.Prof David Clark, a psychologist at the University of Oxford, says he would like to see more people come forward for therapy but says people can also take steps to help themselves.The first step, he says, is to stop obsessive self-focus. "People with social anxiety often monitor themselves constantly during social situations. Am I blushing? Do I sound stupid? Do I look nervous?"Focus outwardly on the conversation, other person or your surroundings."He says you also need to test your fears with behavioural experiments by asking a question in a meeting or saying something in a group and noticing what happens."People with social anxiety often assume negative outcomes – that they will embarrass themselves or think others will find them boring. Testing that can help people break that. It's frightening, but it can really help."He also says they need to drop safety behaviours, such as rehearsing every sentence, avoiding eye contact or sticking close to one particular person.And finally, Clark adds, try to avoid post-event rumination. "It's so easy to distort what actually happened."This is something Mary can empathise with. "I used to play things over constantly in my mind. What I've learnt is that dealing with social anxiety is a gradual process. The therapy really helped me, but so did something a friend said to me a couple of years ago."When I said I didn't want to join her in meeting some of her friends, citing my poor social skills, she said she'd never thought that about me and that I shouldn't undersell myself. I was overcome with emotion."I'm now pushing myself to engage more. It helps that in my postgrad course we're in smaller groups, but I've also joined an astronomy group. It's still difficult and it doesn't always go how I want it to, but I'm learning to manage it."

schema.headline: Social anxiety: The hidden habits that make it worse - and how you can break them

title: Gianni Infantino: Fifa president has 'no place in future of football', says computer hacker Rui Pinto
description: The computer hacker who released documents which led to the Premier League investigation into Manchester City says Fifa president Gianni Infantino "sh
body: The computer hacker who released documents which led to the Premier League investigation into Manchester City says Fifa president Gianni Infantino "should have no place in the future of the game".City have been found guilty of breaching Premier League financial rules over a nine-year period, though they continue to deny any wrongdoing and have until 2 October to submit an appeal.The Premier League investigation was launched following information released into the public domain by the Football Leaks website in 2018, via German publication Der Spiegel, and following a separate investigation by European football's governing body Uefa.In a message on X, external, Rui Pinto, creator of Football Leaks, repeated allegations from 2018 that Infantino intervened to help City and Paris St-Germain avoid financial fair play sanctions from European football's governing body Uefa.According to a report by Der Spiegel, external, the clubs overvalued sponsorship deals to help meet FFP rules and, when facing sanctions over the matter, the allegations in the documents state Infantino helped arrange more lenient punishments for them in 2014.A PSG statement at the time said it "has always acted in full compliance with the laws and regulations enacted by sports institutions" and it "denies the allegations"."Since the introduction of Financial Fair Play, Paris St-Germain have been one of the most audited and scrutinised clubs in history," the club added."Back in 2014, there was a man who was already aware of the irregularities involving Manchester City," 37-year-old Portuguese Pinto wrote on Wednesday."The infamous Gianni Infantino, then Uefa general secretary, abused his authority, shared confidential documents and, in short, outmanoeuvred the investigatory chamber, doing everything in his power to ensure that both Manchester City and PSG would merely receive a fine, avoiding a deeper investigation that could have led to a Champions League ban."All of these details were also revealed through Football Leaks."Given his actions as Uefa general secretary and, more recently, as Fifa president, I can only say, in my humble opinion, that Gianni Infantino has become a cancer on football and should have no place in the future of the game."When the allegations first surfaced, Uefa stressed that it was within the remit of the general secretary to assist in such matters, adding: "This may include discussions, meetings, assistance to help find solutions, and other interactions to assist the [investigating body] in its work."Infantino similarly pointed to how his "job entails having discussions, having conversations, exchanging documents, drafts, ideas, whatever, on many, many, many, many, topics."So if then this is being portrayed as something bad, I think there's not much I can do more than my job in an honest way, in a professional way and trying to defend the interests of football."BBC Sport has contacted Fifa following Pinto's latest statement.Infantino has come under increasing pressure following his now-shelved plans to sell stakes in the World Cup.European football's governing body Uefa accused Infantino of "criminal mismanagement" over the Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) scheme, while the Swiss Football Association (SFV) is the latest association to withdraw its support for the Fifa president."The decision follows a comprehensive reassessment of developments over the past few months," an SFV statement read."From the SFV's perspective, various incidents raise fundamental questions regarding leadership, governance, transparency and decision-making processes within Fifa."Both Fifa and Uefa are based in Switzerland.Infantino will stand for election for a fourth time in March 2027, with his opponents having until 18 November to find an alternative candidate.

schema.headline: Gianni Infantino: Fifa president has 'no place in future of football', says computer hacker Rui Pinto

title: Manchester City charges: Punishment before end of season, Premier League clubs believe
description: Manchester City's punishment for breaching Premier League rules should be handed down before the end of this season, senior football figures have told
body: Manchester City's punishment for breaching Premier League rules should be handed down before the end of this season, senior football figures have told BBC Sport.The Premier League said on Tuesday that City had been found guilty of all charges relating to breaches of its financial regulations between the 2009-10 and 2017-18 seasons.They included artificially inflating revenue by more than £900m through "sham" sponsorship deals.City have repeatedly denied guilt and signalled an intent to lodge an appeal by the end of this week.There have been fears that the process, which has taken three years since City were charged, could be drawn out for much longer.However, senior figures within football have told BBC Sport they see no reason why the case cannot be concluded by the end of this season.Speaking on condition of anonymity, one club official said: "It benefits everyone for this to be resolved as quickly as possible."When asked if they believed it would be, they said: "Instinctively yes, but it has to be done right."We can all see what the risks are if it's not. But those risks have been there throughout the process, as they've won the league multiple times during it."Another source said the process  "should" be resolved by the end of the season, and they hoped any appeal would be "compressed".The final decision rests in the hands of the independent commission, with the Premier League board - and City - able to suggest a suitable punishment before the panel makes its decision.There is increasingly a desire to have the case resolved by the end of the season amid fears that allowing City to get to the end of the campaign without punishment could lead to uncertainty and farce, particularly if they were to win the title.One section of the Premier League regulations says an appeal should conclude no more than 12 weeks after it is filed, and a decision should be made within 30 days of its end.Procedures can be hurried to meet certain deadlines, like the end of a league season.However, Ferran Soriano, the club's chief executive, has suggested the case will run for a long time.Manchester City cannot make a further appeal to the Court of Arbitration for Sport (Cas), but could potentially claim the process was not impartial at the High Court.The Premier League's statement, formally announcing the guilty verdicts read on Monday, said it wants the process to be "concluded as soon as possible".Meanwhile, City club sponsor Etihad Airways said it is considering legal action against the Premier League. In a statement issued on Wednesday, the United Arab Emirates-based airline said it "categorically rejects any finding, conclusion or implication that suggests the airline has ever been involved in improper commercial arrangements".It added: "The Premier League's public communication of the commission's findings, following a period of selective leaks and reporting, has further created damaging implications for Etihad despite the airline not being named in the redacted published findings."Etihad, City's main sponsor since 2009, also said it was given no opportunity to engage in a process that now reflects "adversely on the airline".The statement added: "Etihad is deeply concerned by the way this matter has been communicated publicly. "The lack of clarity and transparency, together with the selective disclosure of information, has created damaging implications for Etihad despite the airline not being named in the published decision. "The Premier League must take responsibility for the consequences of the way in which these findings have been presented."Etihad will seek the relevant legal counsel on the options and recourse available to protect its interests."The Premier League declined to comment when contacted by BBC Sport.

schema.headline: Manchester City charges: Punishment before end of season, Premier League clubs believe

title: Teens who died when car entered River Wear named
description: Two teenage boys and a teenage girl who died when the car they were in ended up in the River Wear have been named by police.Jackson Duke, 17, Luke Eth
body: Two teenage boys and a teenage girl who died when the car they were in ended up in the River Wear have been named by police.Jackson Duke, 17, Luke Etheridge and Zara Shaw, both 16, were in a black Audi A3 that came off the road at Panns Bank near Wearmouth Bridge, Sunderland, and plunged into the water just before 13:30 BST on Tuesday.Jackson and Luke were from Sunderland and Zara was from Houghton-le-Spring, a town about seven miles (11km) from the city. All were students at Sunderland College.Northumbria Police said there were four people inside the car at the time and a 17-year-old boy, who managed to reach safety, had been arrested on suspicion of causing death by dangerous driving.

schema.headline: Teens who died when car entered River Wear named

title: Fury vs Joshua: Heavyweights trade jokes at launch event
description: After more than a decade of public feuding and false starts, Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua exchanged pleasantries, traded jokes and even discussed goi
body: After more than a decade of public feuding and false starts, Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua exchanged pleasantries, traded jokes and even discussed going for a pint at a news conference in London.The British heavyweight rivals will fight at Cardiff's Principality Stadium on 11 December.But for all the history between them, the launch felt more like two veterans in the closing stages of long, turbulent careers taking stock of how far they had both come."He's been a role model and poster boy for British boxing for years," Fury, 38, said of Joshua. "I mostly find myself defending my arch rival to fans in the street."On Monday, there was still uncertainty over whether the fight would happen because of contractual disagreements surrounding the promotion.There had been plenty of reason to expect fireworks on Wednesday. Instead, Joshua, 36, spoke about the magnitude of the event."It's breathtaking and I'm not saying that lightly," he said. "I'm really grateful for this opportunity and bringing it to Great Britain because I know people in pubs have had proper fights about who will win and family members have fallen out."The mood was perhaps best summed up at the face-off, when Joshua smiled and pretended to tickle Fury's stomach.There was something almost surreal about seeing Fury and Joshua finally sitting side by side after so many years in which their rivalry had existed mostly through interviews, social media and failed negotiations.Both had arrived hours earlier for one-to-one interviews. When the news conference began, master of ceremonies Michael Buffer introduced the pair as fireworks shot up from the front of the stage.They entered from opposite sides at the same time - Joshua relaxed and composed in a grey tracksuit and sunglasses, Fury in more flamboyant fashion in a vivid emerald-green suit covered in crown motifs over a white shirt.Alongside the world's media, a few hundred fans filled the balcony above and quickly made their allegiance known as "Oh Anthony Joshua" rang around the British Airways ARC.Joshua has been credited with pushing to keep the fight in Britain and, if Wednesday was any indication, can expect strong backing in Cardiff - even with the main event potentially starting about 02:00 GMT to suit American audiences.For two men whose names have been linked for so long, Fury and Joshua have spent remarkably little time together. But their famous sparring session in 2010, when Joshua was still an amateur, soon became the topic of conversation.Fury suggested he had got the better of it, prompting one fan to shout: "Liar." Joshua smiled and said he could not remember.For those who believe the fight has come years too late, Fury had a simple response. "It's the icing on the cake of two great careers," he said. Moments later, he glanced back at the word "Finally" on the giant screen behind them.There were several moments of common ground. Fury nodded along as Joshua spoke about his Christian faith and, even when the pair traded insults, they rarely felt venomous."This man here is carved in stone and every time he gets cracked on the jaw, he falls over," Fury said."When I crack him on the jaw with a big right hand, he's going down."Joshua laughed and shouted back Fury's own catchphrase: "Get up."The fight has been reported as being for the vacant WBA 'super' heavyweight title, although current WBA heavyweight champion Murat Gassiev's team has lodged a formal objection over the proposed title arrangement.For a moment, it appeared the mood could turn when Joshua revealed he had received a call asking whether Fury's name could appear first in the promotion."You've been crying behind the scenes to get out of this fight. I've checkmated you. You have to fight," Fury replied."I've actually never won a world title here. Now it's on the line, we can become a three-time."That exchange came after several chaotic days in which the role of UFC and Zuffa Boxing chief Dana White had threatened to overshadow the fight.Netflix had presented White as part of the promotion alongside Turki Alalshikh's The Ring, despite Joshua promoter Eddie Hearn insisting his fighter's contract prevented White from having a promotional role.But White did not attend Wednesday's launch. And when Alalshikh thanked the American from the stage, his name was met with jeers from sections of the crowd.Fury did momentarily take aim at Hearn, calling him a "sausage" - but even that did not last long.Within minutes, Fury was offering to go for a pint with the Matchroom boss - and extended the invitation to Joshua."I hope after this fight we can have a pint of Guinness together," Fury said. "Win, lose or draw, let's bury the hatchet.""I don't know if I can trust you," Joshua replied, drawing laughter.The overriding mood was one of relief between two veterans, who were seemingly happy to let the fight settle what years of talk could not.

schema.headline: Fury vs Joshua: Heavyweights trade jokes at launch event

title: Manchester City guilty: What next, how could relegation work and more key questions
description: Criminal investigation? Relegation or expulsion? The key Man City questionsImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Manchester City CEO Ferran Soriano
body: Criminal investigation? Relegation or expulsion? The key Man City questionsImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Manchester City CEO Ferran Soriano (left) and chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak have continued to insist that the club is innocent despite the guilty verdictsByDaniel AustinBBC Sport senior journalistThe verdict that football fans around the world had been awaiting for years is in - Manchester City are guilty.The club still insists it is innocent of the financial rule-breaking charges first brought against it by the Premier League in 2023, and can appeal, so the legal wrangling is far from over.And the verdict has unleashed some huge questions for both the near and long-term future.The Independent Football Regulator (IFR) has said the independent commission's decision raises "serious issues".BBC Sport has taken a look at the key questions in the case and what we know about each of them so far.What happens next and when?The deadline for Man City to make their appeal is Friday. Precedent indicates that City's appeal will be considered and decided upon before punishments are declared.Though that is not guaranteed. And a subsequent appeal against any sanctions could follow.Exactly how long the process - which will be heard by a new three-person commission - will take is as yet unclear.One section of the Premier League regulations says that an appeal should conclude no more than 12 weeks after it is filed, and a decision should be made within 30 days of its end.Procedures can be hurried to meet certain deadlines, like the end of a league season.Man City cannot make a further appeal to the Court of Arbitration for Sport, but could potentially claim the process was not impartial at the High Court.The Premier League's statement, formally announcing the guilty verdicts read on Monday, said it wants the process to be "concluded as soon as possible".The phrasing may not offer any exact insight but the tone - of both the statement, and the strong language used in the independent commission's findings about the length of time the case has taken - is notable."It has taken us much longer than we would have wished, and much longer than we had anticipated would be the case when the hearing concluded, to produce our decision," the commission wrote. "That is regrettable."It is clear that those in charge want the matter wrapped as quickly as can be done.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Erling Haaland's goals have powered Manchester City to the top of the Premier League, but whether they are truly in a title challenge is unclear until sanctions are knownAnd it is arguably to the benefit of both Manchester City and all of the other clubs in the Premier League and English Football League to know where they stand sooner rather than later.City are top of the Premier League, having taken a maximum 15 points from their opening five matches, but whether they are genuinely in a title race will be unclear as long as players, fans, and club owners are in the dark about what their punishment will be.Were the appeal and sanctions process to drag on beyond the end of the season, it would be possible that legal challenges could be brought by teams who finished below City in the table, or are relegated, or were knocked out by them in the domestic cups, which would be far less viable if the club's 'real' position is known before that point.How could relegation or expulsion work?There are two key scenarios here.The first is that one of the sanctions Manchester City are given is so significant a points deduction that they finish this season (or another future campaign, if the process takes longer) in the Premier League's bottom three and are automatically relegated to the Championship.The second scenario is that they are expelled by the Premier League, which would require 15 of their rival clubs to vote in favour of a motion decreeing so.Were that to happen, the club's future would be much less clear and would require them to apply to the Football Association for re-entry. Because the EFL and National League are separate entities from the Premier League, neither would necessarily be obliged to accept an entry request from Manchester City.And, even if a request were accepted by the EFL, its 72 clubs would have to vote whether or not to accept them.That is where the possibility of City beginning a reascent in League Two - or potentially even lower - arises from.There is a huge sporting and financial difference between dropping down to the Championship, with the high possibility of being promoted back to the Premier League after a single season, and starting again far lower down the pyramid.When Juventus were relegated from Serie A to Serie B in Italy, after being found guilty of match-fixing charges in 2006, they were able to retain some of the world's best players, including Gianluigi Buffon, Pavel Nedved and David Trezeguet.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Players like Fabio Cannavaro, Patrick Vieira and Gianluca Zambrotta left Juventus after their enforced relegation, but Gianluigi Buffon stayed and captained the club to the titleThey were willing to put up with a single season in a lower tier and, when the club returned to Serie A after winning the Serie B title, they immediately finished third and qualified for the Champions League.If City faced only a single season outside the Premier League, players on long, lucrative contracts would likely be far more inclined to stay, and the economic damage of losing access to the top flight's TV rights income would be hugely reduced.Could the charges become a legal or criminal investigation?The Fraud Act 2006 states that dishonestly making a false representation with the intention of making a gain or avoiding a loss can lead to individuals being imprisoned for 10 years and facing an unlimited fine, if charges are brought and proven."Surely the Man City findings are now a police matter," said Lord Cruddas, a banker and businessman."If accounts have been falsified and auditors have been misled then it is potentially a criminal matter. The auditors will call in the police, directors are personally liable for any fraud of a UK company even if it is foreign-owned."For the case to move from football wrongdoing to something more, there would first need to be an investigation by the relevant authorities.The bodies who can investigate potential financial crimes in the UK include regional police forces, the National Crime Agency, HMRC and the Serious Fraud Office.BBC Sport has contacted each of those bodies and been given no indication that any kind of investigation has begun, but some do not routinely confirm investigations owing to confidentiality.Greater Manchester Police said: "No referral has been made by the relevant authorities in relation to any alleged criminal offences."But former Manchester City chairman David Bernstein - who left the club five years before its current owners took control - raised the possibility during an interview on BBC Radio 5 Live."This is very serious and I wonder whether some of these issues might need to be referred to authorities outside of the league," Bernstein said."My immediate thoughts are - can the board of directors continue and should the people involved be suspended immediately?"Football finance expert Kieran Maguire feels wider investigation may be unlikely."HMRC might consider it but there is not a lot for them to go on," he said. "There is certainly no corporation tax to recover. Football clubs lose money and City would have lost more money had it not been for the activities it undertook."Could the club's owners be forced out?Fans and pundits have been making the point since news of Manchester City's guilt first broke - if they deliberately flounced the rules over the course of nine years, how can their owners possibly be trusted to run the club moving forward?There is potentially a role to be played by the IFR, which was established in 2025 with the goals of protecting the heritage of English football, ensuring the financial soundness of clubs and promoting resilience in the ownership and spending of clubs.The IFR awards licences to all 116 clubs in English football's top five tiers, which permits them to operate.Club owners, directors and senior executives are subject to an enhanced suitability framework - a beefed-up version of the old-school 'fit-and-proper person's test'.The Football Governance Act 2025 allows the IFR to suspend or revoke licences awarded to clubs as a last resort in cases of wrongdoing."The IFR has powers to assess the suitability of owners, directors and executives and we will use these powers where appropriate, in the interests of protecting the sustainability, honesty and integrity of English football where there is clear evidence of wrongdoing by individuals", IFR chairman David Kogan said in a statement."This includes taking account of findings made by the Leagues. However, as the proceedings remain ongoing between Manchester City and the Premier League we will await further developments."We hope it can be resolved quickly for the sake of fans."And there is another possible scenario too - government intervention.In 2022 Roman Abramovich was forced to sell Chelsea by the UK government, following the launch of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Abramovich's background as an oligarch meant the government froze his assets and threatened to conduct a full seizure.Within three months the club had new owners.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Abramovich had been in charge of Chelsea for almost two decades before he was forced to sell the clubThe Manchester City owners are not subject to any action by the UK government, and all that has been formally declared is that the club broke football financial rules.But the precedent exists that the government can be part of a process in which a football club owner is ousted.Relations between the UK and UAE - whose royal family controls City's ownership group - were previously strong but have weakened to a degree in recent years.Any form of ousting would prove a severe test of diplomacy.

schema.headline: Manchester City guilty: What next, how could relegation work and more key questions
